Hormuz: Iran says three US-escorted tankers hit mines, but Brent falls to its lowest level since August

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three tankers struck mines and caught fire on Monday, November 23, in the Strait of Hormuz. No maritime authority has confirmed it. The same day, Qatar's prime minister was in Washington pushing to revive negotiations, and Brent stayed below $90 [1][2][4][6].
The Revolutionary Guards navy says two tankers hit mines in the eastern part of the strait and a third near the southern coast, and that powerful explosions set all three vessels on fire [1][3].

According to Tehran, the ships were protected by US aircraft: “The US military's air cover did not prevent the incidents,” the statement said, promising videos [3]. No casualties and no ship names were given [3].

No maritime authority has confirmed the incident [4]. On Saturday, three other tankers had already been hit, and tracked traffic through the strait fell to zero on Sunday, according to the National Security Journal website [3][5].
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei vowed to use “all available means” against the US blockade of Iranian ports [2].

On Monday, Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, met Secretary of State Marco Rubio, his second visit to Washington in a few weeks. He believes the region cannot withstand a new round of attacks between the United States and Iran [6][7].
The deadlock persists: Tehran demands the lifting of the blockade before any talks on reopening Hormuz, while Washington demands the complete dismantling of its nuclear facilities [6].
Brent, Europe's benchmark crude, was trading at $88.97 on Tuesday morning in Asia, after its lowest close since August 31, then at $89.49; US crude WTI was at $80.37 [4].
Key takeaway: despite almost daily attacks on tankers, oil prices are falling because the world is producing more than it consumes [4].

According to Deutsche Bank, global oil inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, a surplus of about 1.7 million barrels per day; Libya's Sharara pipeline has also reopened [4]. This surplus is cushioning the Hormuz shock.

Yet the strait keeps emptying: according to tracking firm Kpler, only about 9.5 million barrels per day passed through it over the ten days to November 19, compared with an average of 12.2 million in October [4]. There is also confusion about the ships: Bloomberg spotted a tanker, the Khat Shekan, that appeared to be running the blockade but had no verifiable history [8].
Qatar, itself targeted by Iran during the war and whose economy is suffering from the Hormuz blockade, is the main mediator [7]. But Iran says the contacts “are not yet formal negotiations” [6].
Brent below $90 is good news for your fuel costs and your heating bill, if the drop lasts. But every new explosion in the strait can send prices back up very quickly: the market remains nervous.

Wall Street posts its best session since April 2025, but the head of the New York Fed warns that inflation remains too high, and a December rate hike is seen as almost certain

On Monday, November 23, the S&P 500 jumped 4.73% and the Nasdaq 6.51%, their best day since April 2025. That same evening, John Williams, president of the New York Fed, said inflation was still too high. Markets see a 98% chance of a rate hike on December 9 [1][2][3][5].

Monday's final close: the S&P 500 ended at 7,237.17 points (+4.73%), the Nasdaq Composite at 24,089.56 points (+6.51%) and the Dow Jones at 49,595.31 points (+3.01%) [1]. For both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, it was the best session since April 9, 2025 [1][2].
After seven straight losing sessions, the rebound lifted the S&P 500 out of “correction” territory, meaning a drop of more than 10% from its peak [2].

The same day in New York, John Williams, president of the New York Fed and a permanent member of the committee that sets rates, said persistent inflation is pushing the Fed toward tighter policy, with the pace of hikes depending on upcoming data [3][4].

He expects inflation near 3.5% at the end of 2026, just above 2% in 2027 and back at the 2% target in 2028, with risks “tilted to the upside” [3][7]. Asked about a half-point hike, he replied: “I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action” [3].
The Fed's policy rate currently stands between 3.75% and 4.00%; markets expect another quarter point next month, followed by further hikes in 2027 [3].

According to CME's FedWatch tool, the probability of a quarter-point hike in December rose from about 88% on Friday to about 98% on Monday [5]. The 2-year US Treasury yield rose to about 4.69%, and the 10-year to about 4.93% [5].

Key takeaway: Monday's spectacular rebound does not change the underlying problem. It came mainly from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, whose stock gained 31% [6], not from good news on prices. The Fed, for its part, remains focused on inflation that is too high [3][5].

Williams cites several causes: tariffs, supply chain disruptions, energy prices linked to conflicts in the Middle East and demand driven by artificial intelligence. He believes, however, that the effect of tariffs on prices has largely faded [3].
Next step: the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, due on Wednesday [6]. Then the monetary policy committee meeting on December 8 and 9 [3].

If you hold stocks or a global ETF in your savings or investment accounts, you probably recovered part of last week's losses on Monday. But higher US rates often strengthen the dollar and can push up borrowing costs elsewhere, including in Europe. Don't mistake a record session for the end of the turbulence.

Belgium: 50,000 protesters, tear gas at Brussels-Midi, and still no budget: De Wever warns his coalition could fall on January 1

The national strike day on November 23 brought together about 50,000 people in Brussels according to police, 70,000 according to the unions. Clashes broke out at the end of the march. The same day, Bart De Wever's government broke up without an agreement on €10 billion in savings [1][2][3].
Police counted about 50,000 protesters, the unions 70,000 [1]. The march, organized by the three main unions, protested against the government's savings plan as the cost of living rises [1][2].

In the afternoon, near Brussels-Midi station, police used tear gas and water cannons against several hundred protesters; a metro station was closed [4]. A car was set on fire and AFP journalists saw at least one arrest [1].
La DH reports several arrests and a press photographer struck in the face by a police officer [3].
No planes took off or landed at Brussels-Zaventem and Charleroi between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m., due to a lack of air traffic controllers [1].
Bart De Wever had given himself until November 23 to present a budget to the king [5]. The federal government broke up without an agreement [3].

The prime minister warned on Monday that his coalition could collapse on January 1 without an agreement on €10 billion in savings [1]. He had already offered his resignation to King Philippe on November 2, who refused it [1].
Key takeaway: the street and the coalition are putting pressure on Bart De Wever at the same time, and Belgium risks entering 2027 without a budget or a functioning government [1][3].
The country must reduce a public deficit that is too high under European rules. The government wants to save at least €10 billion in the coming years, notably on pensions [2][6].

The coalition, nicknamed “Arizona,” brings together five Flemish and French-speaking parties with different priorities: some mainly want to cut spending, others refuse to further burden the less well-off. The head of government had already warned that the team could fall if negotiations failed [2].
The mobilization has been going on for months: this is the latest in a series of national strike days and demonstrations [6][1].

If you need to travel to Belgium in the coming weeks, keep an eye on strike notices: the 23rd closed Belgian airspace for 14 hours. A political crisis in Brussels, home of the European institutions, can also delay Belgian files that affect French cross-border workers.

2027 budget: the Senate votes to tax all sick-pay benefits of long-term illness patients, “disgusting” according to the left, and scraps the tax credit for school fees

On Monday, November 23, senators decided by 194 votes to 146 to make the daily allowances paid to patients with a long-term illness (ALD) fully subject to income tax. The government had proposed taxing only half of them. Expected gain: €900 million in 2027 [1][2][3].
The amendment by the budget's general rapporteur, Christine Lavarde (LR), was adopted by 194 votes to 146; the government left it to the “wisdom” of the senators [1][2].
Currently, these allowances, paid during sick leave linked to a long-term illness such as cancer or diabetes, are tax-exempt [3].
According to tax administration estimates, full taxation would bring in €900 million in 2027, compared with €450 million for the government's version, limited to 50% of the allowances [2][3].
The measure had been removed by the deputies before the bill reached the Senate on November 20 [3]. Senators also lowered the tax exemption ceiling on apprentices' wages [3].

They voted to abolish the tax credit for school fees [4]. It is worth €61 per child in middle school, €153 in high school and €183 per university student [5], and benefits more than 2.5 million households [6].

The Senate will vote on the “revenue” part of the budget on November 28, then on the whole bill on December 9; an agreement between deputies and senators must be reached by December 17 at the latest [7].

Key takeaway: the Senate's right-wing majority is going further than the government to find revenue, even if it means targeting sick people, which unites the left and the National Rally against it [2][3].

For Christine Lavarde, the exemption is “not justified in light of the goal of harmonizing the taxation of replacement income”: other sickness benefits are already taxable [3]. The head of the Socialist group, Patrick Kanner, called the amendment “disgusting”; Edwige Diaz (RN-UDR) called it “unacceptable” [2][3].

The Senate right wants a total of about €6 billion in additional efforts compared with the government's bill. It is also targeting the end of the 10% allowance on retirees' pensions, which would bring in €4.7 billion in 2027 [8].

Nothing is final: this is a first-reading vote. The deputies, who rejected the bill, and the senators will then have to reach an agreement, under the threat of a no-confidence vote against the government [7].

If you are on leave for a long-term illness, your daily allowances could become taxable, in full or by half depending on the final version. If you have children in middle school, high school or university, you could lose €61 to €183 in tax credit per child. Nothing is settled before the end of the debate in mid-December.

Choose France: €42.5 billion in investments announced by French companies, of which only €14.9 billion are truly new, on the day private-sector activity shrinks again

On Monday, November 23, the Élysée gathered more than 200 companies for the “France” edition of Choose France: 273 projects worth €42.5 billion, led by ADP (€9.5 billion) and RTE (€8 billion). But only €14.9 billion are new projects, and the same day the PMI index showed a private economy in contraction [1][2][3][5].
The summit, the second edition devoted to French companies rather than foreign investors, presented 273 projects, 81 of them new, for a total of €42.5 billion [1][4].
Of this sum, €14.9 billion corresponds to projects announced for the first time, about 35%; the rest had already been made public [2][3].

The largest project is that of the ADP group, which plans €9.5 billion to modernize Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle and Paris-Orly airports. RTE, which manages the high-voltage grid, announced €8 billion [4][1].
The ecological and energy transition comes first with 67 projects [3]. The Élysée published no figures on jobs created [6].
The 2025 edition had announced 151 projects worth €30.4 billion [3]. The global summit in Versailles in June 2026 had claimed €93 billion in foreign investment [7].
That same Monday, the November flash composite PMI, a monthly survey of purchasing managers, fell to 46.2 from 46.6 in October; below 50, activity is contracting [5].

In manufacturing, the index dropped to 47.9 from 49.5 in October [8]. HCOB, the bank that publishes the survey, cites weak domestic demand and a higher risk of a technical recession in the fourth quarter [9].
Key takeaway: the government wants to show that French companies keep investing despite political uncertainty, but two-thirds of the amounts announced were already known [2][3].

The two largest projects come from state-controlled or regulated companies: ADP for airports, RTE for the power grid [4]. These investments often follow multi-year plans decided in advance, which tempers the “announcement” effect.

The contrast with the economic data is stark. According to Reuters, French private-sector activity is shrinking while Germany's is at a 56-month high [5]. Services, at 46.6, came in below the expected 47.5, and the contraction is the fastest since May [9].
A technical recession means two consecutive quarters of falling GDP. The risk weighs on tax revenue, just as Parliament is examining a 2027 budget built on modest growth.

If you often fly from Roissy or Orly, ADP's €9.5 billion should translate into terminal works in the coming years. The slowdown in activity, meanwhile, can hold back hiring and pay rises at companies that depend on demand in France.

Cyberattack: for a month, hackers suspected of being backed by China have been roaming the European Commission's networks, and it cannot get rid of them

The European Commission suspects a China-backed hacking group of being behind an intrusion into its systems, detected on October 22 and still not under control, Euronews reports. The names and email addresses of EU Academy users have been exposed [1][2][3].
The Commission's IT department spotted a malicious actor in its internal networks on October 22; more than a month later, the attack is still not fully contained [2][3].
Internally, the group goes by the code name “Panda,” according to published reports [2].

The suspicions are based on the sophistication of the attack and on the use of ARTEX, a cybersecurity tool developed in China that uses artificial intelligence to find exploitable vulnerabilities [2][4].
The Commission confirmed that the names and email addresses of users of the EU Academy, its online training platform, were exposed. Theft of staff personal data has not been confirmed [2].
As a precaution, other applications were temporarily disabled, and users are being urged to beware of booby-trapped emails (phishing) [2].
This would be the third China-linked incident targeting the Commission this year [2]. Brussels is refusing for now to officially attribute the attack, as the internal investigation is ongoing [2][1].
Key takeaway: the institution that negotiates trade, sanctions and digital rules for the EU's 27 countries has been spied on for a month without being able to drive out the intruder [1][3].

According to current assessments, the hackers were mainly trying to gauge how deep they could get into the network, rather than targeting specific people or systems [2]. This is typical of state espionage: settling in quietly so as to come back later.
This information is based on anonymous sources: the Commission is not officially accusing anyone. No reaction from Beijing had been published at the time of writing [2][4].
The affair comes at a time of high technological tensions between Europe, China and the United States, where digital infrastructure has become a battleground.

If you have an EU Academy account, your name and email address may have been exposed: be wary of emails that seem to come from the EU and ask you to click a link or give a password. More broadly, you can turn on two-factor authentication on your important accounts.

Boeing: Trump announces 250 more planes for China, but the 200 promised in May still haven't been ordered, as Beijing keeps its planes as a bargaining chip

Donald Trump said on Monday, November 23, that he expects China to buy 250 more Boeing jets. Yet China's commitment to 200 planes made in May has still not been turned into firm orders, and the Shenzhen summit unlocked nothing. According to analysts, Beijing is using it as leverage against US restrictions on chips [1][2][4].
Donald Trump said he expects China to buy 250 more Boeing planes [1]. Boeing did not comment and China has not mentioned any plans for additional purchases [3].
In May, during Donald Trump's visit to Beijing, China committed to 200 planes. Boeing speaks of an “initial commitment,” not an order: these planes do not appear in its official order book [3][5].

Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg explains that Beijing allocates the planes among its airlines, with which Boeing then negotiates one by one. He mentioned about 140 planes “on track” and orders for 10 others being drafted [3][5].
As early as October, Kelly Ortberg had warned that the figure of 250 was not a firm order, only a sign of Chinese interest [5].
According to the South China Morning Post, Donald Trump left China without the 200 planes from May becoming confirmed orders [2][3].

Observers see a tactic: Beijing is said to be using Boeing purchases as leverage against new US restrictions on advanced chips. “Beijing could demand other concessions, on technology or geopolitical rivalry, before placing firm orders,” one of them says [2].
Key takeaway: in China, large aircraft orders are also political decisions. Beijing turns the tap on or off depending on the state of its relations with Washington [2].

China's last big Boeing order dates back to 2017, during a previous visit by Donald Trump: China then signed for 300 planes [2][6]. In April 2025, in the middle of the trade war, Beijing told its airlines to stop ordering Boeing jets [7].

The trade truce between the two countries allows trade to continue, but neither side wants to give up its leverage, CNBC notes. For economist Larry Hu (Macquarie), rare earths are Beijing's main weapon against the US lead in chips [8]. Planes are another.
Observers point out, however, that China's need for new aircraft has not changed [2]: the orders should eventually come, but at a political price.

If Beijing ends up ordering from Boeing, those are planes that won't be bought from Airbus, a large share of which is built in France. These standoffs are also settled on the assembly lines in Toulouse.

Housing: deputies vote this Tuesday on a bill that, against the government's wishes, scraps the bans on renting out energy-inefficient homes

The National Assembly votes this Tuesday, November 24, at 4:30 p.m. on the bill to revive housing. Over the course of the debates, deputies profoundly changed it: an end to the timetable banning the rental of poorly insulated homes, a say for mayors over social housing, and a broader tax break for investors [1][2][3].
The formal vote on the whole “bill on the revival and decentralization of housing” is set for this Tuesday at 4:30 p.m., after the article-by-article review ended on November 20 [3][1].

Against the minister's wishes, deputies scrapped the timetable that gradually banned the rental of “thermal sieves,” homes with poor ratings in the energy performance certificate (DPE) [1][2]. The amendment passed narrowly, by 108 votes to 102 [4].
They gave mayors a right to object to the allocation of social housing in their municipality [1].

They removed the minimum renovation work required to qualify for the “Jeanbrun,” the new tax break for people who buy a home to rent it out [1]. Its article was adopted by 124 votes to 34, with the RN, the Socialists, EPR, MoDem and Horizons in favor, and LFI against [5].
Deputies did, however, reject the reform of the enforceable right to housing (Dalo), which allows people to have their housing needs recognized in court [1].
If the bill is adopted, seven deputies and seven senators will meet in a joint committee to find a compromise. The ministry hopes for final adoption before the end of the year [3].
Key takeaway: the bill coming out of the Assembly is no longer the government's, which makes the outcome of the vote uncertain [3].

Bans on renting out energy-guzzling homes have been divisive for years. Supporters see them as a way to force landlords to insulate and to protect tenants from heating bills. Opponents accuse them of taking homes off the rental market at a time when rental properties are scarce. The six-vote margin shows how divided the Assembly is [4].

The Jeanbrun scheme aims to revive construction and rental investment, which are declining [5][2]. By removing the minimum renovation work, deputies make the benefit easier to obtain, but more costly for the state.
Mayors' say over social housing allocations is a long-standing demand of many local officials, just as their annual congress opens in Paris [1].

If you rent a poorly insulated home, this version of the bill would remove the obligation for your landlord to carry out work before being able to rent it to you. If you are a landlord, you would no longer face a ban deadline. Nothing is final: the Senate still has to reach an agreement with the deputies.

news.2026-11-24-portugal-budget-2027-vot: Portugal: after a record 2,864 amendments, Montenegro's 2027 budget faces its final vote this Tuesday, rescued by the Socialists' abstention

Portugal's Parliament votes this Tuesday, November 24, at 3 p.m. on the whole 2027 budget of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro. The bill, which targets a surplus of 0.1% of GDP and cuts corporate tax, received a record 2,864 amendments. The announced abstention of the Socialist Party should be enough to get it through [1][2][3].
The final overall vote is set for 3 p.m. this Tuesday, after an adjustment to the initial schedule; the article-by-article votes ended on November 23 [1][3].
Deputies examined 2,864 proposed amendments, a record, compared with 2,176 for the 2026 budget [1].
At first reading, on October 28, 89 PSD deputies and two from CDS-PP voted in favor, 79 against, and 60 abstained, including 58 Socialists [2].

The budget targets a public surplus of 0.1% of GDP in 2027, after a balanced budget in 2026, despite a cut in corporate tax from 19% to 18% [2]. The government forecasts 2.1% growth and debt reduced to 84.5% of GDP [4].
During the review, the opposition imposed measures, including a zero VAT rate and the end of the 10% tax rate on landlords' rental income, after wins by the PS [5].
The Left Bloc will vote against and accuses the PS of inconsistency [6]. The small PAN party had warned that it “will not hesitate” to vote against if the government remained “intransigent” [7].
Key takeaway: without a majority, Luís Montenegro is getting his third budget through thanks to the Socialists, who are abstaining to avoid a political crisis [2][3].

The PS chose to abstain with the unanimous backing of its leadership. “Unless there is a surprise that changes the terms of the problem, we will maintain our abstention in the final overall vote,” explained Socialist leader André Moz Caldas [3].

The record number of amendments shows how fragmented Parliament is: each party tries to extract measures in exchange for its vote or abstention [1]. The minority government has to accept some defeats, such as on VAT or the tax on rental income [5].
Portugal stands out in Europe: it is aiming for a budget surplus while France, Belgium and Italy struggle to reduce their deficits [2].

If you have a business or projects in Portugal, the tax on profits is set to fall from 19% to 18% in 2027. If you own a home that you rent out there, the end of the 10% rate on rental income could increase your tax bill.
